parts.name: Mk1 Capsule
parts.desc: One seat, basic life support. Cramped but light.
parts.role: The cabin: one seat, the controls, and the air the crew breathes.
parts.detail: The smallest cabin that keeps a person alive: a seat, a window, life support for the trip and the computer that flies the ship. Shaped like Mercury: a steep cone of dark heat-resistant shingles and a narrow neck that holds the parachutes. Light and cheap, but nothing spare: every extra bottle of oxygen is a separate part outside.
cons: One cramped seat, no spare air
parts.real: Mercury-class: the Mercury capsule was 1.89 m across the heat shield and about 1.3 t in orbit

parts.name: Mk2 Capsule
parts.desc: Roomier cabin, better instruments.
parts.role: The cabin: the crew, the controls and life support, with room to move.
parts.detail: A roomier cabin with better instruments and a little more power. A gentle cone like Gemini and Crew Dragon, with a docking ring on the nose. Still the heaviest single piece of hardware on most ships, which is why it sits on top: the rest of the stack is built to carry it.
parts.real: Gemini (2.3 m) and Crew Dragon (about 4 m)-class cabin: a 20° cone above the heat shield

parts.name: Mk3 Capsule
parts.desc: Big cabin with its own spare oxygen. Heavy.
parts.role: A big cabin with its own spare oxygen. Heavy.
parts.detail: The flagship cabin: more room, more power, a spare oxygen supply built in, and the most reliable systems. A wide blunt cone like Apollo and Orion, so the heat shield is big and the entry is gentle. The price is mass, and mass is paid in propellant.
parts.real: Apollo command module (3.9 m wide, 5.56 t, silver Mylar skin over the ablator) / Orion (5.0 m)

parts.name: Pointed nose, small
parts.desc: A slim ogive for a small stack.
parts.role: A slim nose for a small ship.
parts.detail: A small ogive fairing. Less frontal area means less drag in the thick air of the first two minutes, where most of the aerodynamic loss happens.
cons: Small: looks odd on a wide body

parts.name: Pointed nose cone
parts.desc: Low drag through thick air.
parts.role: A sharp nose that cuts through thick air.
parts.detail: A tangent ogive: a cylinder that curves smoothly into a point, with a boat-tail at the base that narrows down to the capsule's nose. A pointed nose has the least drag in the thick air of the first minutes of flight, which saves propellant and keeps the aerodynamic load low.

parts.name: Pointed nose, large
parts.desc: A big ogive for a wide stack.
parts.role: A big nose for a wide ship.
parts.detail: A large ogive fairing for the widest bodies. More frontal area than the medium one, but the shape still cuts the air cleanly.
pros: Clean shape for a wide body

parts.name: Blunt nose cone
parts.desc: Cheaper and tougher, more drag.
parts.role: A rounded nose: cheaper, tougher, more drag.
parts.detail: A blunt nose is easier to build and takes a hit better, but pushes more air out of the way. The drag costs a little propellant on the way up.

parts.name: Hammerhead fairing
parts.desc: Wider than the body: room for a bulky payload.
parts.role: A fairing wider than the rocket under it.
parts.detail: A hammerhead fairing is wider than the stage below, so a bulky payload fits inside. Its own skin shields what is under it from one debris strike. The price: more drag, and a wide nose pulls the centre of pressure forward, so put bigger fins low.
pros: Shields the top from one hit
cons: Pulls the centre of pressure forward
parts.real: Atlas V 5 m fairing, Delta II 3 m "hammerhead"

parts.name: Payload attach fitting
parts.desc: The cone that bolts the payload to the stage.
parts.role: The standard interface between the payload and the stage under it.
parts.detail: A truncated cone with a bolted ring at the top and a clamp band at the bottom. It carries the whole payload through launch loads, then lets it go cleanly with push-off springs. Every launcher has a standard one, so a payload built for one rocket fits another.
cons: Mass that does no work after separation

parts.name: Spin table & clamp band
parts.desc: Spins the stage above like a rifle bullet before it fires.
parts.role: A turntable that spins the kick motor and payload for stability, and the band that releases them.
parts.detail: Small solid motors have no steering. The spin table turns the motor and payload to about 50 rpm before they separate, so gyroscopic stiffness keeps them pointed during the burn, like a thrown football. A Marman clamp band holds everything until pyrotechnic bolts cut it. Dawn was spun this way before its Star 48 fired.
parts.real: Delta II spin table and 3712 clamp band

parts.name: Kick motor, small
parts.desc: A Star-48 class third-stage motor in the stack.
parts.role: A compact solid motor that adds a final push.
parts.detail: The third-stage motor of the Dawn launch: a titanium sphere of solid propellant with a short nozzle, 66 kN for 87 seconds. Spin-stabilised, it needs no guidance of its own. Here it adds its propellant and thrust to the stack.
pros: Two tonnes of propellant in a small package
cons: Isp 286 s: worse than any liquid engine
parts.real: Star 48B: 66 kN, 286 s, 2,011 kg propellant, 126 kg empty

parts.name: Kick motor, medium
parts.desc: A larger spherical solid motor for the stack.
parts.role: A bigger kick motor: 3.3 t of solid propellant.
parts.detail: The larger spherical motor. Solid motors have the best propellant mass fraction of anything in the hangar (the case is 6 % of the mass), but the exhaust is slow: Isp 290 s.
pros: Best mass fraction in the hangar

parts.name: Ablative heat shield
parts.desc: Chars away to carry the heat off. Heavy and dependable.
parts.role: An ablative shield that chars away to carry heat off.
parts.detail: The ablative heat shield burns slowly and deliberately during entry, carrying the heat away with the charred material. Heavy, dependable, and the only thing between the crew and plasma.

parts.name: Ablative heat shield, large
parts.desc: A wider shield: more drag in thin Martian air.
parts.role: A wide ablative shield: slows the ship harder in thin air.
parts.detail: Mars has so little air that a wider shield matters: more area means more drag and a gentler, cooler entry. This one fits a large stack.

parts.name: Ceramic tiles
parts.desc: Half the mass. Chips if anything hits it on the way up.
parts.role: Ceramic tiles: half the mass, chips if struck.
parts.detail: Ceramic tiles insulate instead of burning away, so they weigh half as much. They are brittle: a piece of ice or foam on ascent can crack them. Columbia was lost in 2003 when launch foam punched a hole in the carbon panels on the leading edge of its wing, and hot gas got in on entry.
cons: Chips if struck on ascent (foam chipped Shuttle tiles on many flights)

parts.name: Inflatable heat shield
parts.desc: A stack of inflatable rings under a woven ceramic cloth. Huge area, new technology.
parts.role: An inflatable aeroshell: the widest shield for the least mass.
parts.detail: Packed small for launch, inflated to a wide cone before entry: stacked rings of woven fabric under a blanket of silicon-carbide cloth. The biggest drag area of any shield, which is exactly what thin Martian air needs. It has flown once, from orbit, in 2022, so reliability is lower.

parts.name: Supersonic parachute
parts.desc: Opens at Mach 1.7 in the thin Martian air.
parts.role: A supersonic parachute for the thin Martian air.
parts.detail: Mars has so little air that the chute opens at Mach 1.7 and still cannot slow the ship enough by itself. It buys time and speed before the engines light for the last kilometres.
parts.real: Perseverance 21.5 m disk-gap-band chute, opened at Mach 1.7 (Viking to Perseverance)

parts.name: Drogue chute
parts.desc: A small, strong chute that opens first and steadies the ship.
parts.role: A small chute that opens early, stops the tumbling and slows the ship a little.
parts.detail: A drogue is small and tough: it can open faster and higher than a main chute, stop the capsule tumbling, and pull the main chute out. Alone it slows the ship only a little; with a main chute it makes the whole descent gentler.

parts.name: Splash floats
parts.desc: Keeps the capsule upright after the splashdown home.
parts.role: Keeps the capsule upright after splashdown.
parts.detail: Inflatable floats for the return to Earth: they keep the capsule the right way up in the sea until the ship arrives.
pros: Keeps the capsule upright at sea
cons: Only matters on the way home

parts.name: Low-gain antenna
parts.desc: Slow but it works from anywhere.
parts.role: Slow but works from anywhere.
parts.detail: A low-gain antenna: no pointing needed, a trickle of data in any direction. Enough for voice, telemetry and small files. Without any antenna nothing you find can be sent home.

parts.name: Medium-gain horn
parts.desc: A horn: faster than the omni, forgiving of pointing errors.
parts.role: A horn antenna: a useful middle between the omni and the dish.
parts.detail: A horn concentrates the signal into a wide cone. It needs only rough pointing, so it keeps working while the ship manoeuvres, and it sends data many times faster than the low-gain stick.

parts.name: High-gain dish
parts.desc: Uploads science fast. Must be pointed.
parts.role: Uploads science fast. Must be pointed.
parts.detail: A high-gain dish sends data hundreds of times faster, but only when it points at Earth. The science of the mission goes home through this.

parts.name: Relay smallsat
parts.desc: A small satellite left in Mars orbit to relay data home.
parts.role: A relay satellite released into Mars orbit: a dish in the sky even when Earth is below the horizon.
parts.detail: Every Mars rover talks to Earth through orbiters overhead. This smallsat rides on the side of the ship, is released into orbit, and relays data from the surface with its own dish and solar panels, so the crew can send science home even when Earth has set.
pros: Fast uploads from the surface, any time of day

parts.name: RCS thruster pack
parts.desc: Small thrusters to turn the ship in space.
parts.role: Small thrusters that turn the ship in space.
parts.detail: A reaction control pack: a cluster of tiny thrusters that fire sideways to roll, pitch and yaw the ship where there is no air for fins to bite. Needed to point the ship for burns and entry.

parts.name: Star tracker
parts.desc: A camera that reads the stars to know which way the ship points.
parts.role: A camera that finds the ship's attitude from the star field.
parts.detail: Gyroscopes drift. A star tracker photographs the sky, matches the pattern against a catalogue of thousands of stars, and tells the computer exactly which way the ship points, to a few arcseconds. Without one the dish and the burns are pointed by dead reckoning. Reliability +0.5 %.
pros: Exact pointing for burns and the dish

parts.name: Reaction wheel
parts.desc: Spins a flywheel to turn without fuel. Slow.
parts.role: Spins a flywheel to turn without fuel. Slow.
parts.detail: A spinning wheel inside the ship: speed it up and the ship turns the other way, no propellant needed. Slow and gentle; good for pointing an antenna, not for a landing.

parts.name: Spare O₂ tank
parts.desc: One EVA refill. A person breathes about 0.84 kg of O₂ a day.
parts.role: One spare EVA oxygen refill.
parts.detail: A high-pressure bottle of oxygen for the suit. A person breathes about 0.84 kg of oxygen a day; one bottle is one refill at the ship between walks outside.

parts.name: Oxygen tank, double
parts.desc: Two refills in one tank.
parts.role: Two EVA refills in one tank.
parts.detail: One tank, twice the oxygen: two refills for the suit. A little lighter than two separate bottles, because one valve and one mounting serve both.

parts.name: CO₂ scrubber
parts.desc: Keeps the cabin air breathable for months.
parts.role: Removes the CO₂ the crew breathes out.
parts.detail: Without a scrubber the cabin fills with carbon dioxide in days. This one works like the ISS scrubber: its beds soak up the carbon dioxide, then are baked clean and used again, so the air stays breathable for months. Apollo 13 used throwaway lithium hydroxide canisters instead.

parts.name: Radiation shelter
parts.desc: Water-walled corner to hide in during a solar storm.
parts.role: A water-walled corner to hide in during a solar storm.
parts.detail: Between the planets there is no magnetic field to hide behind. When the Sun throws a storm, the crew climbs into this shelter, whose walls are tanks of water, until it passes.

parts.name: Water recycler
parts.desc: Recovers about 98 % of the water, like the ISS.
parts.role: Recovers about 98 % of the water.
parts.detail: Turns yesterday's water back into today's. The ISS recovers about 98 %; without it a long trip would need tonnes of water.

parts.name: Radiator panel
parts.desc: Dumps cabin heat into space; vacuum is a thermos.
parts.role: Dumps cabin heat into space.
parts.detail: Vacuum is a thermos: nothing conducts heat away. A radiator panel sheds the heat from electronics and people by glowing it off into space.

parts.name: Escape tower, Mercury type
parts.desc: A solid rocket on a red truss: in an emergency it yanks the capsule off the booster.
parts.role: Pulls the capsule clear of a failing booster in the first minutes of flight.
parts.detail: A three-legged steel truss holds a solid rocket above the capsule. If the booster fails, the motor fires for about a second through three nozzles tilted outward so the flame misses the cabin, and drags the capsule clear; then the capsule's parachutes take over. On a good flight a small jettison motor throws the tower away a couple of minutes up. The real system weighed 460 kg with its ballast; the game's is 350 kg, and since the game drops nothing, it rides to Mars.
pros: Saves the crew in a pad or early-flight explosion
Up to +2 % ship reliability (the whole-ship bonus is capped at 6 %)
Its spike smooths the air over a blunt capsule
cons: Only one escape system counts: a tower and abort pods share one bonus
parts.real: Mercury escape system: Grand Central 1-KS-52000 motor, 52,000 lbf (231 kN) for about 1 s through three canted nozzles; 1,015 lb (460 kg) including 236 lb of ballast

parts.name: Escape tower, Apollo type
parts.desc: A titanium truss with a 650 kN solid motor, canards and a Q-ball nose.
parts.role: Pulls a big command module clear of a failing booster, from the pad to high altitude.
parts.detail: Four titanium legs carry the launch escape motor: four nozzles tilted outward give about 650 kN for three seconds, enough to lift a five-tonne cabin a mile clear. Above it sit the tower jettison motor, a small pitch motor that steers the stack away from the booster, two canards that flip the capsule heat-shield first, and the Q-ball, a nose probe that senses the angle of the airflow. Never needed on an Apollo flight, but carried on every one. The real system weighed about 3.6 t; the game's is scaled down to 4.4 m and 1 t, and since the game drops nothing, it rides to Mars.
pros: Saves the crew from the pad to high altitude
Up to +3 % ship reliability (the whole-ship bonus is capped at 6 %)
cons: Its legs press hard on the nose below it
Only one escape system counts: a tower and abort pods share one bonus
parts.real: Apollo LES: 33 ft (10 m) long, about 8,000 lb (3.6 t); escape motor about 147,000 lbf (654 kN) for 3.2 s; tower jettison motor 31,500 lbf; pitch control motor 2,420 lbf; 10 ft titanium truss

parts.name: Escape tower & fairing, Soyuz type
parts.desc: Tower, fairing and folding grid fins in one escape unit: the system that saved Soyuz T-10a.
parts.role: A fairing over the top of the ship with the escape tower on its nose: in an abort the whole front end flies away with the crew.
parts.detail: On Soyuz the escape tower is bolted to the fairing, not to the capsule. In an abort the motor pulls the fairing and the modules inside it off the rocket, four grid fins fold out to keep it flying straight, and the capsule drops out on its parachute. In 1983 it fired seconds before Soyuz T-10a exploded on the pad: the crew pulled 14 to 17 g and walked away. Small motors on the fairing itself cover the minutes after the tower is gone; they saved Soyuz MS-10 in 2018. The real escape module weighs 7.6 t, but that counts the two crew modules it pulls away; the game's tower and fairing are 1.4 t, and they ride to Mars.
pros: The only escape system that has saved a crew from a pad explosion
Up to +3 % ship reliability (the whole-ship bonus is capped at 6 %)
cons: Big side area high up: pulls the centre of pressure forward
Only one escape system counts: a tower and abort pods share one bonus
parts.real: Soyuz SAS: escape module 7,635 kg, up to 76 t (745 kN) of thrust from about 4 t of solid propellant, four folding stabilisers; Soyuz T-10a (1983), MS-10 (2018)

parts.name: Launch abort system, Orion type
parts.desc: A solid tower with reverse-flow nozzles and its own steering motor: the strongest escape system built.
parts.role: Pulls the crew module away and steers it, from the pad to the edge of space.
parts.detail: No truss: the abort motor stands on a cap over the crew module's nose. Its gas flows up the motor and turns back out through four nozzles near its top, so the tower can be short and the flame starts far from the capsule. Above it are the jettison motor, which pulls the tower away on a normal flight, and at the very top, under the nose cone, the attitude control motor: a ring of eight valves on a solid gas generator that steers the whole stack. Tested on the pad in 2010 and at the worst air load in 2019. The real system weighs about 7 t; the game's is scaled to 1.25 t, and it rides to Mars.
pros: Strongest push of any escape system
Up to +3.5 % ship reliability (the whole-ship bonus is capped at 6 %)
cons: Only one escape system counts: a tower and abort pods share one bonus
parts.real: Orion LAS: abort motor about 400,000 lbf (1.8 MN), attitude control motor up to 7,000 lbf of steering force, jettison motor over 40,000 lbf; Pad Abort-1 (2010), Ascent Abort-2 (2019)

parts.name: Boost protective cover
parts.desc: Fibreglass and cork over the capsule's nose; the escape tower stands on it.
parts.role: Keeps the heat of the climb and the escape motor's flame off the capsule's nose and windows, and carries the tower.
parts.detail: On Apollo a fibreglass shell covered with cork wrapped the whole command module during the climb, so air friction and the exhaust of the escape motor could not scorch the windows and the hatch, and it left with the tower. The game draws only its top: the collar between the capsule's docking tunnel and the tower's legs, 150 kg instead of the real 318 kg.
pros: A solid base for a tower
cons: Mass that does nothing after the climb
parts.real: Apollo boost protective cover: about 700 lb (318 kg) of fibreglass, honeycomb and cork over the whole command module

parts.name: Hinged nose cap
parts.desc: A dome over the docking port that swings open in orbit.
parts.role: Smooths the capsule's nose on the way up and keeps the docking port clean; opens on a hinge in space.
parts.detail: A capsule's nose holds the docking port and its soft-capture ring, which would catch the air on the climb and the heat on the way home. Crew Dragon covers it with a dome that swings aside on a hinge once in orbit and closes again before re-entry. Less drag than a bare nose.
pros: Less drag than a bare capsule nose
cons: A hinge that must close before re-entry
parts.real: Crew Dragon hinged nosecone (Cargo Dragon 1 threw its nose cone away after launch)

parts.name: Recovery nose section
parts.desc: The capsule's own nose: main parachute, re-entry thrusters and a rendezvous radar.
parts.role: A narrow nose on the capsule that packs the main parachute, the re-entry thrusters and a radar for finding other spacecraft.
parts.detail: Gemini had no fairing and no tower: its nose was this section. Inside, the drogue and an 84-ft ringsail main parachute; below them, the thrusters that held the capsule steady through re-entry; on the tip, the radar that found the Agena target for the first dockings. Gemini crews would have escaped on ejection seats instead (an option inside the cabin).
cons: Blunt: more drag than a fairing
parts.real: Gemini rendezvous and recovery section: 84-ft (25.6 m) ringsail main parachute, drogue and pilot chutes, rendezvous radar

parts.name: Von Kármán nose
parts.desc: The least-drag curve for its length and width: less drag than any other nose of its size.
parts.role: A nose shaped by the mathematics of least drag.
parts.detail: Theodore von Kármán worked out the nose curve with the least drag for a given length and base: a slightly rounder tip and a slimmer shoulder than an ogive. The curve bends two ways at once, so its panels are harder to lay up and the price goes up.
pros: Least drag of any medium nose
cons: Compound curves: more expensive to make
parts.real: Haack series with C = 0 (LD-Haack, the von Kármán ogive): the minimum-drag nose for a given length and diameter

parts.name: Biconic nose
parts.desc: Two straight cones: cheap to build from flat panels.
parts.role: A cone on a cone: simple to make, a little more drag than a curved nose.
parts.detail: A biconic nose is two straight cones: a slender one at the base and a blunter one at the tip. Every panel can be rolled from a flat sheet, so it is cheap and quick to make, and the blunt tip stands the heat of a fast climb. The kink between the cones adds a little drag.
parts.real: Cone-on-cone noses on early fairings and sounding rockets; NASA's crewed Mars studies have looked at biconic entry shells

parts.name: Composite fairing, 5 m class
parts.desc: Two carbon-fibre halves around a big payload, thrown off once the air is thin.
parts.role: A large two-piece fairing of carbon fibre on aluminium honeycomb, with a boat-tail down to the capsule.
parts.detail: Big modern fairings are two halves of carbon-fibre skin over an aluminium honeycomb core, joined along a separation rail. Gas pushers or a pyrotechnic cord split them and they fall away. A boat-tail at the bottom narrows to whatever sits under it. Its skin takes one debris strike for what is inside.
pros: Shields the top from one hit
cons: Big side area high on the ship
parts.real: Falcon 9 fairing: 5.2 m wide, 13.1 m tall, carbon fibre on aluminium honeycomb; Atlas V 5-m fairing, 20.7 to 26.5 m long

parts.name: Ablative heat shield, small
parts.desc: A small ablative dish for a one-seat capsule.
parts.role: An ablative shield sized for the small capsule.
parts.detail: Mercury's shield was fibreglass soaked in resin, built up in layers to char away slowly. Small and light, but a small shield means a small drag area: in thin Martian air the ship falls faster and the engines must do more of the braking.
cons: Entry drag area 45 m² against 80 for the medium shield: the engines must brake harder at Mars
parts.real: Mercury orbital heat shield: 1.89 m across, fibreglass and phenolic resin ablator

parts.name: Unpressurised trunk
parts.desc: A hollow section under the heat shield with solar cells and radiators on its skin.
parts.role: The section under the capsule that carries solar cells, radiators and cargo, and joins the capsule to the stage.
parts.detail: Crew Dragon rides on a trunk: an unpressurised cylinder with solar cells on one side of its skin, radiators on the other, and small fins that keep the capsule flying nose-first during an abort. Starliner and Orion use a service module in the same place. Here it adds power and a place to clamp more equipment.
cons: Side area high on the ship
parts.real: Crew Dragon trunk: body-mounted solar cells, radiators and abort fins; thrown away before re-entry

parts.name: Main parachute cluster
parts.desc: Three big ringsail mains in one pack: the ship lands safely on two.
parts.role: Three main parachutes that open together; one can fail and the other two still land the ship.
parts.detail: Crewed capsules hang under a cluster, not a single canopy. Apollo flew three 25.5 m ringsails, and Apollo 15 came down safely on two when one collapsed. Orion flies three, Crew Dragon four. The packs sit side by side and are pulled out together by pilot chutes once the drogues have slowed the capsule.
pros: Twice the drag of one supersonic chute
cons: Opens lower and slower than the supersonic chute
parts.real: Apollo: 3 × 83.5 ft (25.5 m) ringsails; Orion: 3 × 116 ft (35 m); Crew Dragon: 4 mains

parts.name: Abort engine pod
parts.desc: Two hypergolic engines in the capsule wall that push it away from a failing rocket.
parts.role: A pusher escape system: engines built into the capsule instead of a tower on top.
parts.detail: Instead of a tower that pulls, Crew Dragon pushes: eight SuperDraco engines in four pods around its wall, 71 kN each, light within a fraction of a second and shove the capsule clear. Nothing is thrown away on a good flight, and the propellant also feeds the steering thrusters. A set is four pods, one on each side; the reliability bonus counts once for the whole escape system, so pods and a tower together are no safer than the better of the two.
pros: Works from the pad to orbit
Up to +2.5 % ship reliability for the whole set (the whole-ship bonus is capped at 6 %)
cons: 130 kg each, and a set is four
Only one escape system counts: a tower and abort pods share one bonus
parts.real: SuperDraco: 71 kN (16,000 lbf), 3D-printed Inconel chamber, 8 per Crew Dragon in 4 pods; Starliner: 4 RS-88 abort engines at 40,000 lbf (180 kN) each

parts.name: LiOH canisters
parts.desc: Throw-away cartridges that soak up CO₂: simple, cheap, and they run out.
parts.role: Lithium hydroxide cartridges that absorb the carbon dioxide the crew breathes out.
parts.detail: Cabin air is blown through lithium hydroxide, which binds the carbon dioxide; when a cartridge is full it is swapped for a fresh one, about every twelve hours. No power, nothing to break, but they are used up. Apollo 13's crew had to tape the command module's square canisters into the lunar module's round sockets.
cons: Used up: enough for weeks, not months
parts.real: Apollo command module LiOH canisters (square; the lunar module's were round); still a backup on the ISS
